title: Subtitles, dubbing and what gets lost

turns.speaker: Marco
turns.text: Apparently half the subscribers here watch English-language shows with the subtitles on. Their own language, subtitled.

turns.speaker: Ellis
turns.text: That's me, actually. The sound mixing on a lot of new drama is genuinely unintelligible.

turns.speaker: Pia
turns.text: That's a real thing. Dialogue gets mixed for cinema and then played through a television speaker the width of a pencil.

turns.speaker: Marco
turns.text: The more interesting question is dubbing though. Countries split on it and nobody really knows why.

turns.speaker: Ellis
turns.text: Size of the market, mostly. Dubbing is expensive, so small language markets subtitled and got used to it.

turns.speaker: Pia
turns.text: And there's a decent correlation between subtitling countries and English proficiency, which nobody can prove is causal.

turns.speaker: Marco
turns.text: It's suggestive, though. Thousands of hours of hearing a language while reading what it means is not nothing.

turns.speaker: Ellis
turns.text: Dubbing defenders would say you lose the picture while you read.

turns.speaker: Pia
turns.text: Which is true for maybe a week, and then you stop noticing you're doing it.

turns.speaker: Marco
turns.text: The thing I'd actually defend dubbing for is children and anyone who reads slowly. It isn't only snobbery on the other side.

turns.speaker: Ellis
turns.text: No, that's fair. And good dubbing is a craft. The bad kind is what gives it the reputation.

turns.speaker: Pia
turns.text: What I object to is a country only ever offering one. Give people the switch.

turns.speaker: Marco
turns.text: Which streaming actually solved, more or less by accident.

points: About half of subscribers watch shows in their own language with subtitles on, partly because modern dialogue mixing is hard to hear on television speakers.
Ellis explains the dubbing and subtitling divide largely by market size, since dubbing is expensive for small language markets.
Pia notes a correlation between subtitling countries and English proficiency that cannot be shown to be causal.
Marco argues exposure to a language alongside its meaning is likely to help.
Pia dismisses the objection that reading costs you the picture, saying viewers adapt quickly.
Marco defends dubbing for children and slower readers, and they agree the real fault is offering only one option, which streaming largely solved.
